guard: the handler takes the broker's own `.fire` and lets the checkpoint plane judge it, so a pause nobody answers actually expires
why: THE DEFECT WAS AN ABSENT CALLER, and every suite that should have caught it supplied one by
hand. `handleCheckpointFire` is the function that turns the broker's fire into the settlement
the fire names, and nothing outside the suites called it. Each timeout cell in mesh-sleep,
mesh-wait and mesh-checkpoint called it directly, so what they graded was that the checkpoint
plane expires a pause WHEN SOMEBODY DELIVERS ITS FIRE. That was true, and it was never the
question. Reproduced on a live broker with nothing hand-delivered: a two-second sleep, the timer
writer arming one schedule, the broker publishing `.fire` on the token's own subject, and four
seconds later the status still `waiting`, the settle fact ABSENT, and the effect still pending.
Durable, correct, and permanent.
A TEST THAT DOES THE SUBJECT'S WORK FOR IT GRADES ITSELF. That is the general shape and it is
worth more than the fix: the injected call sat in a helper named for what the broker does, so it
read as scaffolding rather than as the mechanism under test. The helpers are now OBSERVATIONS --
`brokerFired` asks whether the broker published, and nothing delivers anything.
TWO CALL SITES, ONE MECHANISM, and they are graded separately because they fail apart. `sleep`
and `checkpoint` await a settle fact through the watcher, so they pump the fire alongside the
wait. `wait` POLLS its deadlines, so it takes the fire on the same poll it was already making.
Mutation 4 removes only the polling half: the sleep suite stays green and every wait with a
timeout waits past its timeout forever.
THE CLOCK MATTERS AND THE SUITES HAD TO CHANGE FOR IT. Expiry is a judgement about the owner's
clock against a durable absolute deadline, so the handler judges the fire with the clock it was
given. Two suites pinned that clock to one reading so a deadline could be named exactly -- and a
clock frozen BEFORE its own deadline judges every real fire premature and re-arms the schedule
instead of expiring it, forever. Neither smoke could have shown that while it was expiring the
pause itself. The pinned clock is now advanced when real time passes, and the checkpoint suite's
expiry block runs its own handler on a moving clock.
EVERY CELL THAT ASSERTS TERMINATION CARRIES ITS OWN DEADLINE. `mutation-proof` grades a hang
INCONCLUSIVE -- "a hang is not a red" -- so a guard against a pause that never ends, asserted by
a bare `await`, grades nothing at all: the suite stops, the tool declines to call it, and the
mutation goes unscored. `withDeadline` turns the hang into a named red.
SPECIFIER BOUNDARY: checked rather than assumed. All three suites import the mutated module
through a relative `../src/*.js` path and every command is bare `tsx` with no build step, so the
bytes mutated are the bytes the suites load. The `@cotal-ai/core` and `@cotal-ai/lang` imports in
these files resolve to `dist`, which is why no mutation here targets either package.
THE SMALLEST EDIT THAT STILL BREAKS THIS AND STILL PASSES, named rather than left to be found:
changing `FIRE_POLL_MS` from 2_000 to something enormous. Every cell here still passes, because
each waits long enough for one poll, and a pause would then expire minutes late in production.
It is not given a mutation because the cells cannot distinguish a slow pump from a prompt one
without asserting a latency, and a latency assertion on a real broker is a flake. It is a
CONSTANT this file names, not a branch, and it is called out here so the next reader knows the
guard proves the fire is taken and not how soon.

mutations.name: the pump is never started: `settle` waits on the watcher alone, which is the shipped state
mutations.completionMarker: • 1 — the pause is durable and exactly one schedule was armed
mutations.expectRed: the sleep effect did not end within 20000ms
mutations.cell: the sleep effect did not end within 20000ms
mutations.note: The exact shipped state, reproduced on a live broker before the fix. It reddens as a wait that never ends rather than as a wrong answer, which is why nothing was red for as long as it was: the pause is durable and correct in every observable way except that it is permanent.

mutations.name: the pump checks once and gives up, so it only ever works if the deadline already passed
mutations.completionMarker: • 2 — the same step after a crash
mutations.expectRed: both waiters did not end within 20000ms
mutations.cell: both waiters did not end within 20000ms
mutations.note: The half-fix that passes a reading. A single look at mint time finds nothing, because the fire is published at the deadline and the wait begins before it -- so the pump has to be a pump. Graded on the second block, where two waiters attach to one pause, so it names a different cell from mutation 1.

mutations.name: the fire is read at a neighbouring epoch, so a live fire is invisible on the wrong subject
mutations.completionMarker: • 1 — the pause is durable and exactly one schedule was armed
mutations.expectRed: the sleep effect did not end within 20000ms
mutations.cell: the sleep effect did not end within 20000ms
mutations.note: A fire belongs to the instance and epoch that armed it, and the subject carries both. This is the one-character version of the defect: everything about the pump is present and correct and it is listening one epoch away. It matters because a run ADOPTED at a new epoch re-arms at the new coordinates, so a pump bound to the wrong one is exactly the takeover case.

mutations.name: the polling half is removed, so a `wait`'s timeout is read for and never produced
mutations.completionMarker: • 5 — the wait's timeout is minted, armed, and past due
mutations.expectRed: the timed-out wait did not end within 25000ms
mutations.cell: the timed-out wait did not end within 25000ms
mutations.note: The two call sites fail apart, and this is the one a fix written from the sleep report alone would miss. `wait` never awaits a settle fact through the watcher; it POLLS for one, which means it reads for a fact only it can produce. With this applied the sleep suite is entirely green and every wait with a timeout, and every idle window, waits forever.

mutations.name: PAIRED: the pump is never started, graded on `checkpoint` rather than on `sleep`
mutations.completionMarker: • 3 — nobody answers: the deadline is armed and past due
mutations.expectRed: the run did not end within 30000ms
mutations.cell: the run did not end within 30000ms
mutations.note: Same edit as mutation 1, a different suite, and it is here because the two effects are not the same claim. A `sleep` is a pause nobody will ever answer; a `checkpoint` has a resolver, and its expiry is the case where the resolver did not come. Graded through the run driver end to end, so what reddens is a RUN that does not finish rather than an effect that does not return.

unkillable.name: that a fire handed over twice is harmless
unkillable.why: It is a property of the checkpoint plane's one-use settlement, not of this file: the second hand-over finds the pause already settled and declines. It is graded in `packages/core/smoke/endpoint-checkpoint.smoke.ts`, where the verdicts themselves are the subject. A mutation here would be aimed at code this change does not own.

unkillable.name: the `re-armed` verdict under owner-behind clock skew
unkillable.why: It needs a host clock genuinely behind the broker's, which these suites cannot produce without freezing the handler's clock -- and a frozen clock is the state that re-arms forever, so the fixture and the failure are the same thing. What the suites DO carry is the consequence: `armPending`'s fetch window is short so it cannot straddle a deadline and count a correct re-arm as a second arming.
